Friendship and social life

Why is it so hard to make friends as an adult?

At school, friendship arose almost by itself. As adults we lack what feeds it most: shared time and repeated encounters.

In childhood and at university we made friends almost without trying. With work, partners, children or moving cities, many people find their circle has shrunk and that making new friends is very hard.

A matter of hours

In 2019, the researcher Jeffrey Hall studied adults who had moved and students starting university. He estimated that it takes about 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 to become friends and over 200 to become close friends. Time counts more if spent talking and doing things together than sharing a space without interacting.

Adult life lacks the repeated, unplanned encounters that school or halls of residence provided. We also tend to underestimate how much we are liked: in 2018, Erica Boothby and colleagues described the liking gap: after a conversation with a stranger, people believed they had made a worse impression than they actually had.

People like us more than we think

After a conversation with someone new, we tend to think they liked us less than they actually did. Erica Boothby and colleagues called this the liking gap: in their studies, people consistently underestimated how much their conversation partner liked them and enjoyed the conversation. Knowing this can encourage you to take the next step, such as suggesting meeting again.

People are glad to hear from you

We often do not write to an old friend because we think they will find it odd or not care. A 2022 study by Peggy Liu found that people who received an unexpected message from someone they had lost touch with appreciated it much more than the sender had predicted. A short message, with no need for an excuse, is usually well received.

What usually helps

  • Look for settings that repeat: a club, volunteering, a class, a team.
  • Take the step of suggesting a concrete plan: many friendships stall at "we should meet up".
  • Be consistent: friendship grows with frequency.
  • Remember the liking gap: they probably liked you more than you think.
Friendship is not a luxury: lack of social relationships is associated with worse health and higher mortality, with an effect comparable to other well-known risk factors.

References

  1. Hall, J. A. (2019). How many hours does it take to make a friend? Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 36(4), 1278–1296.
  2. Boothby, E. J. et al. (2018). The liking gap in conversations. Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756.
  3. Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B. y Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
  4. Boothby, E. J., Cooney, G., Sandstrom, G. M. y Clark, M. S. (2018). The liking gap in conversations: do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756.
  5. Liu, P. J., Rim, S., Min, L. y Min, K. E. (2023). The surprise of reaching out: appreciated more than we think. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 124(4), 754–771.
